To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) rats will self-administrate nicotine to the point where they exhibit signs of dependence and (2) the pattern of nicotine intake is altered in the presence of a 23 h light/dark cycle.

(1) nicotine self-administering rats exhibit a dose-dependent increase in nicotine intake and a decrease in lever responding; (2) nicotine decreases food intake and alters circadian patterns of feeding; (3) somatic signs of nicotine withdrawal are precipitated by mecamylamine and are positively correlated with the amount of nicotine self-administered; and (4) extinction of nicotine self-administration is facilitated by the absence of cues associated with nicotine self-administration.

rats with 23 h access to nicotine self-administration develop nicotine dependence, as evidenced by the development of somatic signs of nicotine withdrawal, the development of a nicotine-seeking behavior resistant to extinction, and the development of a circadian profile of food intake that mimics the pattern seen in nicotine-dependent humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rat model of nicotine dependence.
the development and maintenance of nicotine addiction.
the effects of nicotine on food and water intake in rats with access to nicotine self-administration.

rats with 23 h/day access to nicotine self-administration will develop a dependence syndrome, and that this dependence is characterized by somatic signs of nicotine withdrawal, resistance to extinction of nicotine-seeking, and changes in circadian patterns of feeding behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rats self-administer nicotine in order to maintain a stable level of nicotine intake, and that the amount of nicotine intake is a major determinant in the development of nicotine dependence.

rats will self administer nicotine to the point where they are dependent on nicotine and this dependence is manifested in a variety of behavioral and physiological measures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rats were self-administering nicotine to the point where they became dependent on it, as measured by withdrawal signs and resistance to extinction, as well as measures of food intake.
the circadian profile of food intake is disrupted by nicotine self-administration, and the disruption is dose-dependent.
